items.title: extensions
items.text:
Optional packages for the canVODpy ecosystem

Each of these packages does one job alongside canVODpy. Install only the one you need: a naming recipe for the files your receiver writes, an Airflow DAG for a site's daily runs, or an adapter to exchange data with another GNSS-T program.

Start here Contribute

items.title: Packages
items.text:
• canvod-filemap

    Maps the files your receiver writes to their canVOD file names, so a run finds your data without you renaming anything on disk.

    Naming recipes

  • canvod-airflow

    One daily DAG per site, plus one to backfill a date range. The tasks run the code of canvodpy run.

    Airflow DAGs

  • canvod-adapters

    Reads and writes observations and VOD for another GNSS-T program, for example gnssvod, and checks each import against canvodpy's contracts.

    Data exchange

canVODpy is a lean core that works fully without any of these packages. Each one is optional, installs on its own, and follows its own release cadence. For the packages canVODpy ships and how to set a site up, see canVODpy.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: Contributions are welcome. This guide covers the development setup and contribution workflow.

items.title: Required tools
items.text: Two external tools must be installed separately (not managed by uv sync):

items.title: The uv package manager
items.text:
# macOS/Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Or via package manager
brew install uv

uv documentation

items.title: The just command runner
items.text:
# macOS/Linux
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://just.systems/install.sh | bash

# Or via package manager
brew install just

just documentation

items.title: Report bugs
items.text: Report bugs at https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy-extensions/issues. Include your operating system, your setup, and the steps to reproduce.

items.title: Fix bugs and implement features
items.text: Issues tagged "bug"/"enhancement" and "help wanted" are open for contributions.

items.title: Add a new package
items.text: New extension packages live under packages/<name>/ and are picked up automatically by the uv workspace (packages/*). Each package is versioned on its own and published to PyPI (see Releasing below). A package lists every dependency it needs, with no extras. See packages/canvod-filemap for the expected layout (pyproject.toml, src/, tests/, README.md).

items.title: Development workflow
items.text:
1. Install required tools (uv and just).

  2. Fork and clone the repository: 

    git clone git@github.com:your_name_here/canvodpy-extensions.git
cd canvodpy-extensions

  3. Install dependencies: 

    uv sync
just hooks

  4. Create a feature branch: 

    git checkout -b name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature

  5. Make changes and verify: 

    just test
just check

  6. Commit using conventional commits: 

    git commit -m "feat(filemap): add support for recipe overrides"

  7. Push and create a pull request: 

    git push origin name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature
    A maintainer reviews and merges it. Coding agents may push the feature branch and open the pull request, but never merge, push main or tags, or bypass a check (AGENTS.md, Git and GitHub).

items.title: Commit message format
items.text:
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

Types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci

Scopes: filemap, airflow, adapters, deps, ci, docs, release

Examples: 

git commit -m "feat(filemap): add recipe-based mapping for non-canonical filenames"
git commit -m "fix(filemap): handle missing site config gracefully"
git commit -m "docs: update installation instructions"

See Conventional Commits for the full specification.

items.title: Common commands
items.text:
just --list                    # Show all commands
just test                      # Run all tests
just test-coverage             # With coverage report
just check                     # Lint + format + type-check

items.title: Coding agents
items.text: AGENTS.md (root and per package) holds the instructions for coding agents; the CLAUDE.md files import it. Task guides for agents are in .claude/skills/. Keep them correct when you change what they describe; just check-agent-docs checks that the paths and recipes they name exist.

items.title: Pull request guidelines
items.text:
1. Include tests for new features. New code must not reduce test coverage.
  2. Update the package's README.md and the Zensical documentation in docs/ if adding or changing public API or behavior.
  3. Ensure compatibility with Python 3.14+.
  4. Add yourself to CONTRIBUTORS.md if this is your first contribution.

items.title: Licensing
items.text: canvodpy-extensions is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. By submitting a pull request, you agree that your contribution is licensed under the same terms. The LICENSE and NOTICE files at the repository root apply to all source files. Per-file license headers are not required.

items.title: Code quality
items.text:
• ruff for linting and formatting
  • ty for type checking
  • pytest for testing with coverage

Run just check before committing.

items.title: Releasing
items.text:
Releases are cut by a maintainer, never by a coding agent; only maintainers can create release tags.

Each package is versioned and released on its own. A release is the git tag <package>-v<version>, for example canvod-filemap-v0.2.0, on main.

just versions                         # current version of every package
just changelog canvod-filemap         # changes since its last release
just release canvod-filemap minor     # or major, patch, or for example 0.2.0

just release runs the package's tests and makes one commit that

  • sets the version in packages/<package>/pyproject.toml (and uv.lock),
  • writes packages/<package>/CHANGELOG.md from the commits that changed packages/<package>/ (git-cliff, cliff.toml).

Commit messages become the changelog, so follow the commit convention here and mark breaking changes (feat!: or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer).

main requires a PR (branch protection), so the tag is set after the merge:

git checkout -b chore/release-canvod-filemap-0.2.0   # before just release
just release canvod-filemap 0.2.0
git push -u origin chore/release-canvod-filemap-0.2.0
gh pr create --fill
# once merged:
git checkout main && git pull
just tag canvod-filemap                # tags main and pushes the tag

(Don't tag before the PR merges: a merge can produce a different commit SHA than the one you tagged, orphaning the tag.)

Pushing the tag runs release.yml, which checks that the tag matches the package version and drafts a GitHub Release with the tag's section of the package's CHANGELOG.md. Publish the draft by hand. Publishing archives the repository on Zenodo, versioned by the tag: .zenodo.json and CITATION.cff carry no version, since the packages have different ones. Then raise the lower bound downstream (canvodpy's filemap group) if the release needs it.

Then publish the package to PyPI by running publish_pypi.yml on the tag:

gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref canvod-filemap-v0.2.0

It checks that the tag matches the package version, builds the package without the workspace's [tool.uv.sources], refuses a dependency on a URL (PyPI rejects those) and uploads with PyPI trusted publishing, so no token is stored anywhere. The upload waits for a maintainer's approval of the pypi environment. A package's dependencies must all be on PyPI first.

A new package under packages/ needs one step on PyPI before its first upload: add a pending trusted publisher for the package name (owner TUW-GEO, repository canvodpy-extensions, workflow publish_pypi.yml, environment pypi). The first upload creates the project and turns the pending publisher into a normal one. PyPI can refuse a second pending publisher while one is pending; then upload that package first. In the repository, the package's first just release starts its changelog and tags.

items.title: How a release works
items.text: This page documents the release chain of the extension packages, from commit message to PyPI upload. The steps to follow are in Contributing. canVODpy's own chain is in How the release infrastructure works; the extensions differ in one point: each package is released on its own, with its own version, tag, GitHub release, and PyPI upload.

items.title: 1. Conventional commits
items.text: Commit messages follow type(scope): subject, for example fix(filemap): handle an empty recipe file. The commit-msg hook (installed by just hooks) runs commitizen's check and rejects other messages. The messages become the changelog, so mark breaking changes (feat!: or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer).

items.title: 2. Versions, changelogs, and tags
items.text:
Recipe What it does just versions Prints the version of every package just changelog canvod-filemap Prints the package's changes since its last release just release canvod-filemap 1.1.0 Runs the package's tests, sets the version (major, minor, patch, or a version number), writes the package's CHANGELOG.md, and makes one release commit just tag canvod-filemap On an up-to-date main, tags the package's version and pushes the tag

Changelogs. Every package has a CHANGELOG.md in its folder. git-cliff (cliff.toml) writes it from the commits that changed packages/<package>/. Edit the new section in the release pull request where an entry is wrong or missing: the draft release takes its notes from it.

Tags. A release is the tag <package>-v<version>, for example canvod-filemap-v1.1.0. just release refuses a version whose tag exists already. just tag refuses to tag unless main matches origin/main and the package's CHANGELOG.md has a section for the tag, so a tag always points at a merged release commit.

main requires a pull request, so the release commit goes through one: just release on a branch, pull request, merge, then just tag on main. Tagging before the merge can leave the tag on a commit that never reaches main.

items.title: 3. Draft releases
items.text:
.github/workflows/release.yml runs when a tag canvod-*-v* is pushed:

  1. Reads the package and version from the tag and stops if the tag names no package under packages/ or doesn't match the package's version.
  2. Takes the release notes from the tag's section of the package's CHANGELOG.md, as edited in the release pull request, and stops if there is none.
  3. Creates a draft release titled <package> <version> (a pre-release for a, b and rc versions).

A maintainer reviews the draft and publishes it. Publishing archives the repository on Zenodo, versioned by the tag. .zenodo.json and CITATION.cff carry no version, since the packages have different ones.

items.title: 4. PyPI publishing
items.text:
.github/workflows/publish_pypi.yml runs only when started by hand, on a release tag:

gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref canvod-filemap-v1.1.0

Tagging and publishing to PyPI are separate decisions: a tag isn't a promise that PyPI has the version.

Build job (no upload permission):

  1. Stops unless it runs on a tag, the tag names a package under packages/, and the tag matches the package's version.
  2. Builds exactly that package with uv build --no-sources: as PyPI users get it, without the git sources of [tool.uv.sources].
  3. Refuses a wheel with a dependency on a URL (pkg @ git+https://...), which PyPI rejects.

Publish job: runs in the GitHub environment pypi. The environment needs a maintainer's approval before the job starts, and accepts only tags canvod-*-v*. The job uploads with uv publish --trusted-publishing always.

Dependencies first. Every dependency of a package must be on PyPI before the package can be installed from there. The extensions depend on canVODpy packages (canvodpy, canvod-utils and others), so a canVODpy release that an extension needs goes to PyPI first.

Uploads to PyPI are permanent: a version can't be uploaded twice, so a broken release is fixed by the next patch version.

items.title: 5. Trusted publishing with OIDC
items.text:
The publish job proves to PyPI which repository, workflow, and environment it runs in, with a short-lived token from GitHub; no PyPI token is stored anywhere. The details are in canVODpy's OIDC trusted publishing explained.

Each package is its own project on PyPI and needs the trusted publisher once:

Owner:             TUW-GEO
Repository name:   canvodpy-extensions
Workflow name:     publish_pypi.yml
Environment name:  pypi

New package: a package that isn't on PyPI yet has no project to add the publisher to. Add a pending publisher instead, under Publishing in your PyPI account settings. It takes the package name and the four fields of the preceding block. The first upload creates the project and turns the pending publisher into a normal one. PyPI can refuse a second pending publisher while one is pending; then upload that package first.

items.title: Complete example
items.text:
Releasing a fix in canvod-filemap:

git switch main && git pull origin main
just changelog canvod-filemap
git switch -c chore/release-canvod-filemap-1.0.1
just release canvod-filemap patch
git push -u origin chore/release-canvod-filemap-1.0.1
gh pr create --fill
# merged once CI passes, then on main:
git switch main && git pull origin main
just tag canvod-filemap
# draft release "canvod-filemap 1.0.1" appears: review, publish
gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref canvod-filemap-v1.0.1
# approve the pypi environment when GitHub asks

Users then update with uv add canvod-filemap==1.0.1.

items.title: Release commit refused
items.text: Tag <tag> exists already: choose the next version. Commit or discard your changes first: just release needs a clean working tree.

items.title: Tag refused
items.text: main differs from origin/main: git pull first. <tag> is not in packages/<package>/CHANGELOG.md: the release commit isn't on main yet; merge its pull request first.

items.title: Draft release missing
items.text: The tag must have the form <package>-v<version> and match the version in packages/<package>/pyproject.toml on the tagged commit.

items.title: PyPI workflow fails at once
items.text: Run this workflow on a release tag: start it with --ref <package>-v<version>, not on a branch.

items.title: Upload refused by PyPI
items.text: Check that the project on PyPI has the trusted publisher of section 5, with the same repository, workflow file, and environment name. A package that isn't on PyPI yet needs a pending publisher.

items.title: Domain docs
items.text:
How the engineering skills should consume this repository's domain documentation when exploring the codebase.

canvodpy-extensions shares canvodpy's domain (GNSS-T, sites, files, stores). So its words are canvodpy's: there is no second glossary here.

items.title: Before exploring, read these
items.text:
• canvodpy:GLOSSARY.md: the project's words, in canvodpy at the locked commit (just canvodpy-ref).
  • canvodpy:docs/adr/index.md: canvodpy's decisions. Read the ones about the area you're about to work in.
  • docs/adr/ in this repository, once it exists: decisions that concern only the extensions.
  • CODING_STANDARDS.md: the rules every change follows.
  • The AGENTS.md of every package you change: where things live, invariants, tests.

items.title: Where new terms and decisions go
items.text:
• A new term goes into canvodpy's GLOSSARY.md, through a pull request in canvodpy. The extensions never define a word of their own.
  • A decision that concerns only the extensions (how a package works, what it supports) gets an ADR in this repository's docs/adr/, numbered from 0001, with a row in docs/adr/index.md. Create the folder with the first ADR.
  • A decision that changes canvodpy too (a contract, a public name canvodpy imports) gets its ADR in canvodpy.

items.title: Use the glossary's vocabulary
items.text:
When your output names a domain concept (in an issue title, a refactor proposal, a hypothesis, a test name), use the term as defined in canvodpy's GLOSSARY.md. Don't drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If the concept you need isn't in the glossary yet, that's a signal: either you're inventing language the project doesn't use (reconsider) or there's a real gap (note it for /mattpocock-skills:domain-modeling, and add the term in canvodpy).

items.title: Flag conflicts with an ADR
items.text:
If your output contradicts an existing ADR, here or in canvodpy, surface it explicitly rather than silently overriding:

Contradicts canvodpy ADR-0007 (provenance in log books), but worth reopening because…

items.title: Issue tracker
items.text: Issues and specs for this repository live as GitHub issues. Use the gh command-line tool for all operations.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• Create an issue: gh issue create --title "..." --body "...". Write a body of several lines to a file and pass it with --body-file.
  • Read an issue: gh issue view <number> --comments, filtering comments by jq and also fetching labels.
  • List issues: gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]' with appropriate --label and --state filters.
  • Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent: gh issue create --parent <parent> ..., or gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child> afterwards (gh 2.94+). Older gh: gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id> (database id, as in Blocking below). Without sub-issues, put Part of #<parent> at the top of the child body.
  • Comment on an issue: gh issue comment <number> --body "..."
  • Apply / remove labels: gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..." / --remove-label "..."
  • Close: gh issue close <number> --comment "..."

Infer the repository from git remote -v; gh does this automatically when run inside a clone.

items.title: Pull requests as a triage surface
items.text:
PRs as a request surface: no. (Set to yes if this repository treats external PRs as feature requests; /mattpocock-skills:triage reads this flag.)

When set to yes, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the gh pr equivalents:

  • Read a PR: gh pr view <number> --comments and gh pr diff <number> for the diff.
  • List external PRs for triage: gh api --paginate 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open' --jq '.[] | select(.author_association | IN("OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR") | not) | {number, title, author: .user.login, author_association, labels: [.labels[].name]}'.
  • Comment / label / close: gh pr comment, gh pr edit --add-label/--remove-label, gh pr close.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare #42 may be either: resolve with gh pr view 42 and fall back to gh issue view 42.

items.title: When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"
items.text: Create a GitHub issue.

items.title: When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"
items.text: Run gh issue view <number> --comments.

items.title: Operations of the wayfinder skill
items.text:
Used by /mattpocock-skills:wayfinder. The map is a single issue with child issues as tickets.

  • Map: a single issue labeled wayfinder:map, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. gh issue create --label wayfinder:map.
  • Child ticket: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (see Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put Part of #<map> at the top of the child body. Labels: wayfinder:<type> (research/prototype/grilling/task). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the person driving it.
  • Blocking: the native issue dependencies of GitHub, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>, where <blocker-db-id> is the blocker's numeric database id (gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id, not the #number or node_id). GitHub reports issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a Blocked by: #<n>, #<n> line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
  • Frontier query: list the map's open children (gh issue list --state open, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0, or an open issue in the Blocked by line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
  • Claim: gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me, the session's first write.
  • Resolve: gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>", then gh issue close <n>, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

items.title: Triage labels
items.text:
The skills speak in terms of five canonical triage roles. This file maps those roles to the actual label strings used in this repository's issue tracker.

Label in mattpocock/skills Label in this tracker Meaning needs-triage needs-triage Maintainer needs to evaluate this issue needs-info needs-info Waiting on reporter for more information ready-for-agent ready-for-agent Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent ready-for-human ready-for-human Requires human implementation wontfix wontfix Not acted on

When a skill mentions a role (for example "apply the AFK-ready triage label"), use the corresponding label string from this table.

Edit the right-hand column to match whatever vocabulary you actually use.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text:
Interfaces of the adapters, one per kind of data canvodpy exchanges.

A tool implements the interfaces of the data it exchanges with canvodpy, and only those. Everything entering canvodpy is checked against canvodpy's own contract for that kind of data:

  • observations: :func:canvod.readers.validate_dataset, the contract of every canvodpy reader. Observations are imported with a reader of the tool's files, a :class:canvod.readers.GNSSDataReader.
  • VOD: :func:canvod.readers.validate_vod_dataset, the contract of VOD calculator output and of the VOD store.

A subclass converts; checking the result and recording provenance is done here, the same for every tool.

items.title: gnssvod
items.text:
Adapters between canvodpy and gnssvod (Humphrey et al.).

canvodpy reader of gnssvod observation files.

Conversion between canvodpy and gnssvod (Humphrey et al.) data.

gnssvod Observations: dims (Epoch, SV), one variable per RINEX observation code (S1C, C1C, L1C, D1C; RINEX 2: S1, P2, ...), plus Azimuth and Elevation in degrees (Observation objects, gnssvod.preprocess). VOD: dims (Epoch, SV), one variable per band named in the bands argument of gnssvod.calc_vod, which merges the band's observation codes present in the data in sorted order (numpy.intersect1d), each filling the gaps of the previous.

canvodpy dims (epoch, sid), sid "SV|BAND|CODE" with the coordinates sv, system, band, code and the band frequencies; SNR, Pseudorange, Phase, Doppler, VOD; theta (polar angle from zenith) and phi (azimuth from North, clockwise) in radians.

Signal IDs and observation codes are mapped with :func:canvod.readers.gnss_specs.obs_codes.sid_for_obs_code and :func:~canvod.readers.gnss_specs.obs_codes.obs_code_for_sid, the rules of canvodpy's RINEX readers. Angles: Elevation = 90 - degrees(theta), Azimuth = degrees(phi) mod 360.

See the Overview for usage.

items.title: GnssvodObservations
items.text:
Bases: ObservationsAdapter

gnssvod observation files <-> canvodpy observations.

Attributes:

Name Type Description time_system str

Time scale of the epochs of the gnssvod files to import, as in the RINEX files they came from; only "GPS" is accepted; see :class:~canvod.adapters.gnssvod.reader.GnssvodObsReader.

Examples:

>>> adapter = GnssvodObservations(time_system="GPS")
>>> obs = adapter.import_file("ROSA_obs.nc")
>>> adapter.export_file(obs, "back_obs.nc", source="ROSA_obs.nc")

items.title: GnssvodVod
items.text:
Bases: VodAdapter

gnssvod VOD files <-> canvodpy VOD.

A gnssvod VOD file is the result of gnssvod.calc_vod for one station pair (DataFrame.to_xarray()) written as NetCDF: dims Epoch, SV, one variable per band, Azimuth/Elevation.

Attributes:

Name Type Description bands dict[str, list[str]]

gnssvod's bands argument: band variable to the signal-strength observation codes calc_vod merges into it, e.g. {"VOD_L1": ["S1C", "S1W"], "VOD_L2": ["S2W"]}. Importing gives each band's VOD the sids of its code if the band has one code ("S2W" -> "G01|L2|W"), and of its RINEX 2 form if it merges several ("S1" -> "G01|L1|u", canvodpy's marker for a band whose tracking code is not known). Exporting merges canvodpy's VOD the same way as calc_vod, a merged band also taking the sids an import gives it, so imported VOD exports unchanged.

time_system str

Time scale of the epochs, as in the RINEX files gnssvod read (their TIME OF FIRST OBS record). canvodpy stores every epoch in GPS time, so only "GPS" is accepted; files in another time scale are refused when imported. Recorded on the epoch coordinate, like the readers do.

Notes

calc_vod reports the reference receiver's Azimuth/ Elevation; canvodpy reports the canopy receiver's. Imported VOD keeps gnssvod's angles.

Examples:

>>> adapter = GnssvodVod(bands={"VOD_L1": ["S1C", "S1W"]}, time_system="GPS")
>>> vod = adapter.import_file("vod_canopy_vs_reference.nc")

items.title: Package
items.text:
canvod-airflow: Airflow DAG definitions for canvodpy GNSS-T pipelines.

See daily_processing.py (one daily DAG per site) and backfill.py (manual date-range backfill DAG). No pipeline logic lives here; every task wraps a stateless function from canvodpy.workflows.tasks.

daily_processing.py and backfill.py import airflow at module level (apache-airflow is a dependency of this package), since these modules only ever run inside an Airflow scheduler process. canvodpy-side config/task imports are deferred inside each DAG-construction function instead, so a missing or misconfigured canvodpy config doesn't crash DAG parsing.

The DAG modules are documented by hand

daily_processing.py and backfill.py import airflow at module level, which is required to build the TaskFlow DAGs, so mkdocstrings cannot import them in an environment without Airflow. Their public interface is described below by hand instead.

items.title: daily_processing
items.text: One factory builds the daily DAG of a site. Importing the module builds one DAG for every site in canvodpy's settings file.

items.title: create_daily_dag(site_name: str, agency_ephemeris: bool)
items.text:
Builds the daily DAG of site_name, scheduled daily. Chain: validate_dirs → wait_for_data → (wait_for_sp3) → process_day → validate_ingest → calculate_vod.

When agency_ephemeris is true, the DAG also waits for the SP3/CLK products before it processes the day.

items.title: canvod_backfill
items.text:
A manually triggered DAG that accepts site, start_date, and end_date (YYYYDDD format) as Airflow parameters. It expands the date range into one t_process_day task per date. The tasks run with max_active_tis_per_dagrun=1.

See the Overview for the usage examples.

items.title: Recipe
items.text:
Naming recipe: user-defined mapping from arbitrary filenames to canVOD names.

A recipe is a small YAML file that describes: 1. The canonical identity of a receiver (site, agency, sampling, etc.) 2. How to extract date/time fields from the user's physical filenames.

The field extraction is a sequential left-to-right walk over the filename. Each entry in the fields list consumes characters and either extracts a named value or skips literal characters.

Recognized field names

  • year 4-digit year (e.g. 2025)
  • yy 2-digit year (80-99 → 19xx, 00-79 → 20xx)
  • doy day of year (1-366)
  • month month (01-12)
  • day day of month (01-31)
  • hour hour (00-23)
  • minute minute (00-59)
  • hour_letter RINEX 2 session letter (a-x = hours 0-23; 0 = daily file)
  • skip ignore these characters

Example recipe (YAML)

::

name: fangorn_reference
description: Orthanc, reference receiver

site: FAN
agency: INK
receiver_number: 1
receiver_type: reference
sampling: "05S"
period: "15M"
content: "AA"
file_type: rnx

glob: "*.??o"

# Example: rref001a15.25o
fields:
  - skip: 4
  - doy: 3
  - hour_letter: 1
  - minute: 2
  - skip: 1
  - yy: 2
  - skip: 1

Example recipe for exotic filenames

::

# Example: STATION_2025_042_00_15.rinex
fields:
  - skip: 8
  - year: 4
  - skip: 1
  - doy: 3
  - skip: 1
  - hour: 2
  - skip: 1
  - minute: 2
  - skip: 6

items.title: canvod-adapters
items.text: canvod-adapters exchanges data between canvodpy and other GNSS-T programs. Every import is checked against canvodpy's contract for that data, and every conversion records where the data came from. The package adapts gnssvod.

items.title: When you need it
items.text: You need it when another GNSS-T program writes your observations or VOD, or when you want to give yours to it. You don't need it when you only read and write canvodpy's own readers and stores.

items.title: Install
items.text: uv add canvod-adapters

items.title: A minimal example
items.text:
gnssvod works on datasets whose axes are the epoch and the satellite, with one variable per RINEX observation code (S1C, C1C) or per VOD band, and angles in degrees. canvodpy works on the epoch and the Signal ID, for example G01|L1|C, and angles in radians. The adapter maps one to the other.

Import a gnssvod VOD file into the VOD store, and export one back:

from canvod.adapters.gnssvod import GnssvodVod
from canvod.adapters.store import export_vod, import_vod

adapter = GnssvodVod(bands={"VOD_L1": ["S1C", "S1W", "S1X"], "VOD_L2": ["S2W"]}, time_system="GPS")

import_vod(adapter, "gnssvod_vod.nc", site.vod_store, "canopy_01_vs_reference_01")

export_vod(
    adapter,
    site.vod_store,
    "tau_omega_zeroth_order/canopy_01_vs_reference_01",
    "vod_canvodpy.nc",
)

items.title: How it fits into a run
items.text:
The package separates what every program shares from what is specific to one program, behind one interface per kind of data.

One interface per kind of data. Programs exchange different data with canvodpy: one writes observations, another only VOD. A program's adapter implements the interfaces of the data it exchanges, and only those.

canvodpy's contracts guard everything that comes in. canvodpy defines what its data looks like, and the interfaces check every import against it:

Data Contract Observations canvod.readers.validate_dataset, the contract of every canvodpy reader VOD canvod.readers.validate_vod_dataset

Observations come in through a reader of the program's files (a canvod.readers.GNSSDataReader), so they carry the same file hash, attributes and epoch time scale as observations read from RINEX or SBF files. See Building a reader.

Settings are Pydantic models. An adapter is a frozen Pydantic model whose fields are the program's settings, checked when the adapter is created, for example the bands of GnssvodVod.

Provenance. Every conversion records the program, its URL and installed version, the canvod-adapters version, the direction, the source and the time in the dataset attributes (conversion_*), read back with Provenance.from_attrs.

items.title: Limits and known issues
items.text:
• gnssvod's calc_vod merges the observation codes of a band. Imported VOD of a band with one code gets the Signal IDs of that code (S2W → G01|L2|W). A band with several codes gets canvodpy's marker for an unknown tracking code (G01|L1|u).
  • calc_vod reports the reference receiver's Azimuth and Elevation. canvodpy reports the canopy receiver's. Imported VOD keeps gnssvod's angles.
  • The VOD store keeps imported VOD under the program's name, apart from the VOD canvodpy computed. Importing the same file again is skipped.
  • gnssvod keeps the epochs of the RINEX files it read, in observation and in VOD files, so the files' time scale is a required setting (time_system). canvodpy stores every epoch in GPS time, so a file in another time scale is refused rather than converted.

items.title: Another program
items.text:
To add an adapter for another program:

  1. Create a subpackage canvod.adapters.<program>.
  2. Describe the program with a Tool (name, Python distribution, URL).
  3. Implement the interfaces of the data it exchanges: VodAdapter (open, save, convert_to_canvodpy, convert_from_canvodpy) or ObservationsAdapter (reader, convert_from_canvodpy, save).
  4. Put the program's settings in fields of the adapter.

Contract checks, provenance and store I/O come with the interfaces.

items.title: API
items.text: See the API reference for the full public API.

items.title: canvod-airflow
items.text: canvod-airflow turns canvodpy's task functions into Airflow DAGs. One daily DAG per site runs the site's processing, and one backfill DAG covers a date range. Every task calls canvodpy.workflows.tasks, so no pipeline logic lives here.

items.title: When you need it
items.text: You need it when a site's processing runs on a schedule you don't want to start by hand, or when you want to reprocess a date range you already ran. You don't need it when you run canvodpy run yourself, or when you process one batch once.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add canvod-airflow

This also installs apache-airflow>=3.3.2, the first release without known vulnerabilities; an installed Airflow older than that is upgraded. Airflow runs on POSIX systems (Linux, macOS); on Windows, run it in WSL2 (Airflow's prerequisites).

items.title: A minimal example
items.text:
Point a dags_folder at a shim module that imports both DAG modules, so Airflow's DagBag finds them. Airflow's pre-filter scans the folder for DAG files. Give the shim a name that holds the keywords, for example canvod_dags.py:

# <dags_folder>/canvod_dags.py
from canvod.airflow.daily_processing import *  # noqa: F403  (Airflow DAG scan)
from canvod.airflow.backfill import *  # noqa: F403

Importing the module builds the DAGs. For each site in canvodpy's settings file, the package builds a daily DAG named canvod_{site}:

t_validate_dirs → t_wait_for_data → (t_wait_for_sp3) → t_process_day → t_validate_ingest → t_calculate_vod

t_validate_dirs checks the receiver directories. t_wait_for_data and t_wait_for_sp3 are sensors: they wait until the files of the receiver and the satellite products are there, holding up to 21 days. t_process_day reads the files and stores the observations, t_validate_ingest checks them, and t_calculate_vod computes the VOD.

To reprocess a date range, trigger canvod_backfill by hand with the site and the range:

airflow dags trigger canvod_backfill --conf '{
    "site": "fangorn",
    "start_date": "2025001",
    "end_date": "2025010"
}'

Each date becomes one mapped task. A failure on one date retries only that date; the rest of the range continues.

items.title: How it fits into a run
items.text:
The tasks call canvodpy's task functions directly: validate_data_dirs, check_day, check_sp3_availability, process_day, validate_ingest, and calculate_vod. These functions are stateless and accept only primitives, so they carry dates and settings to and from Airflow. Use them in a script or a notebook without Airflow if you want.

The daily DAG waits for SP3/CLK products only when a run uses agency ephemerides, that is when processing.params.ephemeris_source is not broadcast. With broadcast, the satellite angles come from the SBF files themselves and the results are available the same day. See Configuration. Parallel processing and Icechunk stores explain how the runs scale and write.

items.title: Limits and known issues
items.text:
• An Icechunk store takes one commit at a time. Every task that writes to a store uses the pool canvod_store_write with one slot, which serializes the writes across the DAGs and the backfill runs. Create the pool once: 
    airflow pools set canvod_store_write 1 "Serialise Icechunk commits"
  • Within one backfill run, the dates process one at a time (max_active_tis_per_dagrun=1).
  • The settings file must be reachable from the Airflow worker. If it is not, no DAGs are generated.

items.text: See the API reference for the full public API.

items.title: canvod-filemap
items.text: canvod-filemap gives a receiver a naming recipe: a description of how the receiver's own filenames translate to canVOD filenames. A run then finds the receiver's files without you renaming anything on disk.

items.title: When you need it
items.text:
canvodpy run processes files whose names follow the canVOD filename convention, in any folder layout. If your receiver writes files with other names, for example Septentrio SBF files, legacy RINEX v2 short names, or a custom layout, set a naming recipe on the receiver.

You don't need it when your files already follow the convention, or when a run already finds them.

items.title: Install
items.text: uv add canvod-filemap

items.title: A minimal example
items.text:
A naming recipe is a YAML file, kept per site in the configuration directory at <config dir>/recipes/<site>/<name>.yaml. Load it, then map one file:

from pathlib import Path

from canvod.filemap import NamingRecipe

recipe = NamingRecipe.load(Path("config/recipes/fangorn/fangorn_reference.yaml"))
vf = recipe.to_virtual_file(Path("rref001a15.25o"))
print(vf.canonical_str)  # the canVOD filename; the file on disk keeps its name

The recipe reads the receiver identity, the date, and the sampling from the receiver's own filename and writes them as a canVOD filename. CanVODFilename of canvod-preflight parses and builds the names, the same class a run uses. Before a run, check which files it would process:

canvodpy config validate --site fangorn

items.title: How it fits into a run
items.text:
A run uses the naming recipe only for a receiver whose settings set a recipe. Reference it on the receiver in canvod-settings.yaml:

sites:
  my_site:
    receivers:
      reference_01:
        recipe: my_site_reference

A run finds the files in any folder layout and takes each file's day from its name. See the canVOD file naming convention and Configuration.

items.title: Recipes from a link
items.text:
A recipe can live in a GitHub repository, so that every machine uses the same one. Set the raw link of the file, at a commit, a tag or a branch:

        recipe: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<recipes-repo>/<commit>/my_site/my_site_reference.yaml
  • Any raw link. The link names a commit, a tag (refs/tags/<tag>) or a branch. You are responsible for what it points to.
  • Checked like a local recipe. The recipe's name must match the filename at the end of the link. A github.com/.../blob/... link is refused, and the message names the raw link.
  • Provenance. The store records the filename at the end of the link, never the link, and the sha256 of the file it was made with.
  • Fetched by every run. There is no cache: every run fetches the recipe again, once, into a folder of the run that only you can read. A run without network access stops and names the link.
  • Private repositories. Public recipes need nothing more. A recipe in a private repository needs a GitHub token that can read it, in GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN; a fine-grained, read-only token for that one repository is enough. A variable that holds no valid token stops the run with a message that names the variable, not its value. canvodpy never stores the token, sends it only to raw.githubusercontent.com, and refuses a link that holds a user name, password, query, or fragment. Keep the token where you keep other secrets (the system keychain, a password manager, the secrets store of your scheduler), and start the run with it in the environment.

items.title: Limits and known issues
items.text:
• A recipe has no layout field: a run finds the files in any folder layout and takes each file's day from its name. An older recipe that still sets layout loads, and the field has no effect.
  • Fields a recipe holds that canvod-filemap does not know are ignored. canvodpy config validate lists them as unrecognized, and a run logs them.
  • Recipes from a URL are read only from raw.githubusercontent.com.
  • A recipe saved directly in <config dir>/recipes/ is not used. The error says where to move it. It belongs in <config dir>/recipes/<site>/.
  • A recipe does not change that compressed files are never processed.
  • DataDirMatcher and PairDataDirMatcher in canvod-readers are obsolete and the next major version removes them.

items.title: Start here
items.text:
These packages are optional add-ons for canVODpy. Start here when canVODpy already works on your data and your setup needs one of them.

Each is on PyPI and installs on its own:

You need Install Read next Your receiver's files don't follow the canVOD filename convention canvod-filemap Naming recipes A site's processing to run on a schedule canvod-airflow Airflow DAGs Another GNSS-T program to read or write your observations and VOD canvod-adapters Data exchange

items.title: Install a package
items.text: Add the package to the project that uses canvodpy. Each package brings everything it needs.

items.title: canvod-filemap
items.text: uv add canvod-filemap

items.title: canvod-airflow
items.text:
Install it wherever the DAGs run. It also installs Apache Airflow 3; an Airflow 3 that is already installed is used as it is:

uv add canvod-airflow

items.title: canvod-adapters
items.text: uv add canvod-adapters

items.title: If you don't install a package
items.text:
canVODpy imports canvod-filemap only for a receiver whose settings set a naming recipe (recipe:). Without a recipe, a run takes only the files with canVOD filenames, even when the package is not installed. A receiver with a recipe but without the package stops the run with an error that says how to install it. It never guesses the filenames. See Optional extensions.

canvod-airflow and canvod-adapters call canVODpy, not the other way around. A run never needs them.
